name: Fatima Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so please tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a usual working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Fatima, 43, and lead the container-loading software team at a tech company. My master's taught me the theory, but the useful part is walking a dock supervisor through a trailer mismatch before a driver leaves the yard. I use AI daily for test cases and compare them with signed loading sheets. My partner maintains rail equipment, and our two children are in school; the mortgage makes any move a family calculation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues the AI helper is good at finding repeated loading mistakes, but the dock crew knows when a container is actually on the wrong truck. I use it every day for test data and still check the signed loading sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays a small helper, I think my lead job is safe. My salary is typical, my partner has steady work maintaining rail equipment, we have about four months of expenses saved, and there are some other software firms nearby; the mortgage fits our present wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reviewing the container-loading code with the dock supervisor before releases. In the first year we'd add 120 to our emergency account each payday while both wages hold, and I'd keep the AI tests on fake container numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our income. I would spend the saved hour fixing the screen that tells a driver the wrong gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the signed sheet catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the dashboard put a chilled container on a dry-goods truck. The signed loading sheet had the right trailer number while our test trusted the wrong screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your children make of the repeated checks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two children ask why I check numbers again at home. I say getting the right box to the right place is part of respecting the people waiting for it.

I'd ask dock staff to flag **wrong-gate screens** before release.
think: I expect **my lead wage** to hold under limited AI change.
I have **four months saved**, two steady wages and some local job options.

Use **fake container numbers** in current AI tests.
Save **120 each payday** while both wages hold.
feel: **Calm** about household money, focused on wrong-gate mistakes.

fieldNote: **Stable partner pay** and four months saved make the mild scenario manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI could plan loading, write fixes and answer drivers, so our firm should show the dock crews what changes before it cuts developers. I would put an AI loading plan beside the real trailer sheet and see which one the crew trusts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lead a new checking process, or I could be given fewer hours after the tool does most of the planning. Four months saved gives us time, but a mortgage and two children mean I cannot treat a cut as an interesting experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our operations head for permission to run AI plans on old loading days, with dock workers marking every wrong trailer and driver delay. If the error rate is lower and the crew agrees, I'd introduce a checked plan for one lane in the first year; we'd postpone replacing our roof tiles until my paid hours are clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the team, though I like making a tool prove itself in the yard. The people who lift the boxes should get to say when the screen is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which case could stop the pilot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start with the chilled container that went to dry goods. If the AI repeats it, I would stop the one-lane trial before a driver follows the wrong gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can wait on the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The roof repairer says the tiles can last another season if we patch the leak now. We would pay for the patch, but not a full replacement while the firm weighs staffing.

I'd ask for **wrong-trailer counts** beside speed claims.
think: I could lose **paid lead hours** after AI takes planning.
I have **four months saved**, but a cut would pressure the mortgage.

feel: **Anxious** about wages, interested in a genuine yard test.

fieldNote: **Planning and code** are exposed, so her own paid hours may shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2028 reaches loading plans and code before hands-on robots spread around 2031. A driver still needs a clear human answer when the wrong trailer is assigned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead software post could go when one cheap system plans and checks loads. My partner's rail wage and four months of savings keep the mortgage paid briefly, but the nearby developer market may shrink at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd list mortgage, school and moving costs with my partner and ask two distant logistics firms about paid code-integration jobs. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd accept a signed offer only if its wage with my partner's confirmed transfer covers those bills and the move; without that transfer, I'd search paid remote work from our current home rather than pull the children out of school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I could pack boxes quickly, but I cannot move our family on the strength of a recruiter saying a post might open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a partner transfer already arranged?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner's rail employer has sites elsewhere, but no transfer is promised. We'd ask for a written decision, and we would not put the house up for sale until both jobs and the children's school place were real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about a possible move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children that a move is one option on paper, not a plan for next Monday. They deserve their school year to stay steady while adults check wages.

I'd ask who answers drivers after a **wrong trailer assignment**.
think: I expect **my lead post** could disappear quickly.
I have **four months saved**, but the local market may shrink with us.
do: List **family costs** for mortgage, school and moving with my partner now.

feel: **Alarmed** about job loss and an unpromised family move.
S2.quote: I cannot move our family on the strength of a recruiter saying a post might open.
fieldNote: **2028 thinking AI** threatens code and plans before robots reach hands-on loading.
A family move requires **two written jobs**, bill-covering wages, moving costs and a real school place.

steps.text: Ask distant logistics firms for signed integration offers after a cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years until 2031 gives families time to decide whether staying near the dock or moving for work makes sense. Robots follow around 2034, but thinking AI reaches our code first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might find a better paid developer role in a larger market, but a new city could also cost more. I would not spend our four-month reserve on moving without a wage offer and my partner's transfer; my current software post still faces 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the rail employer for written transfer rules this year, then compare actual rents, school places and code-integration salaries in two cities. If both employers offer signed jobs and the net household pay covers mortgage or rent, moving and school costs, we'd choose a move before 2031; in the first year after AI arrives I'd keep the new post only while it pays enough, otherwise I'd seek another paid role before using savings for a second move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the coding job, but five years let us make a decision from documents instead of panic. I would not ask the children to change schools on a maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as a good enough moving offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Net pay is what remains after rent, travel and childcare, not the salary on a job advert. We would write the numbers down together and ask the schools whether places are actually open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the rail transfer fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the rail transfer falls through, I would stay here and apply for paid remote roles. I would not ask my partner to give up a steady wage for my experiment.

I'd tell families to compare **net wages** and school places before moving.
think: I might gain **better developer pay** in another city, but costs could eat it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 lets us decide from work and family numbers rather than a headline. Thinking AI reaches code in 2036, while robots follow around 2039 for physical loading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might be leading a different software team, or I might be looking for work. Our current wages and four-month cushion make the next few years feel secure, though I cannot promise which city will have paid developer jobs in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking loading releases with the dock crew and save 120 each payday while both wages hold. We'd review our mortgage and any real job offers every year; in the first year after 2036 I'd change employers only for a signed role whose household pay covers housing and school costs, wherever we live then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the present. We can make each decision when an actual offer and school place exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you leave in the loading record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loading record would include the chilled container, wrong trailer and the dock scan that corrected it, without a driver's private details. I want the next developer to see why the fast plan sent a chilled container to the wrong trailer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your older child about study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our older child asks whether to learn coding or a trade. I'd say try both kinds of work and look for a paid apprenticeship if the practical work appeals to them; no forecast can choose for them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because code and loading plans could cheapen before we have a second location worked out. Written job offers for both adults, moving support and confirmed school places would make a move reviewable.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what happens when the dock crew says our screen is wrong. I want their signed sheet beside every AI loading plan. The person moving the container should never have to argue with a dashboard alone.

headlineQuote: The person moving the container should never have to argue with a dashboard alone.
portrait: Fatima, **43**, leads container-loading software after a master's degree and tests plans against signed dock sheets.
Her **typical pay**, partner's rail wage and four-month cushion support a mortgage and two school-age children.
She uses AI **daily** but trusts a dock scan after a chilled container was sent to the wrong trailer.
Steady disruption makes her **anxious** about hours; fast 2028 AGI alarms her about the job and a possible move.
With more time, she compares **two-city offers** and moves only with signed jobs, school places and family costs covered.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her lead post before a signed family move is possible.
whatWouldHelp: **Two written offers**, moving support and confirmed school places would make relocation feasible.
